title: “RESIST THE DEVIL AND HE WILL FLEE FROM YOU” — BUT THE WORDS BEFORE THAT PROMISE MAY EXPOSE THE VERY THING YOU REFUSE TO SURRENDER
paragraphs: “RESIST THE DEVIL AND HE WILL FLEE FROM YOU” — BUT THE WORDS BEFORE THAT PROMISE MAY EXPOSE THE VERY THING YOU REFUSE TO SURRENDER
You keep rebuking the devil, but have you surrendered to God? The terrifying truth about James 4:7, the doors we leave open, and the grace of Jesus Christ that can change everything.
There is a frightening possibility that many Christians never seriously consider.
You can spend years telling the devil to leave while refusing to surrender the very thing God has been telling you to let go.
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, someone will whisper, “Satan, get behind me,” while secretly planning to return to the same sin tomorrow.
Someone will pray for deliverance from temptation while keeping the phone number that keeps pulling them back into darkness.
Someone will ask God to restore their marriage while refusing to surrender their pride.
Someone will beg Jesus for peace while continuing to feed the bitterness that has been poisoning their heart for years.
And someone will declare, with absolute confidence, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you!”
They know the verse.
They have memorized it.
They have posted it on Facebook.
They have probably even encouraged someone else with it.
But there is something deeply uncomfortable about the way that verse is often quoted.
We love the promise of the devil fleeing. We are not always as eager to embrace the command that comes before it.
And if you are willing to stay with me through this, you may discover that the greatest spiritual battle in your life is not simply about what the enemy is doing around you.
It may also involve what you have been unwilling to surrender within you.
The apostle James wrote:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — James 4:7, KJV
Notice what comes first.
Not resistance.
Not shouting.
Not spiritual confidence.
Submission.
And that one word changes the entire conversation.
The original Greek begins:

Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ θεῷ
Hypotagēte oun tō theō.
“Submit yourselves, therefore, to God.”
Then comes:

ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.
Antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
“But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
These are not two disconnected inspirational sayings.
They belong together.
The Greek verb hypotagēte comes from hypotassō, meaning to subject oneself or submit to authority. In this passage, it calls believers to place themselves under God's rightful authority.
The word antistēte comes from anthistēmi, meaning to stand against or resist.
And pheuxetai means “he will flee.”
James is not giving us a magical phrase to repeat until Satan becomes frightened.
He is commanding a posture of life.
Submit to God. Stand against the devil.
Both commands matter.
And the promise belongs within that context.
But to understand why James speaks so forcefully, we must look at the people he was addressing.
Because James was not writing to a room full of people who openly worshiped Satan.
He was confronting people whose desires, conflicts, and divided loyalties were tearing apart their spiritual lives.
Earlier in the chapter, he asks:
“From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?” — James 4:1, KJV
Think about that.
Before James tells believers to resist the devil, he confronts the desires battling within them.
Their quarrels.
Their selfish ambitions.
Their envy.
Their prayers shaped by wrong motives.
Their friendship with a world system opposed to God.
James 4:4 even describes spiritual unfaithfulness using the shocking language of adultery.
Then James declares that God gives more grace and opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
Only after that does he say, “Submit yourselves therefore to God.”
That little word “therefore” matters.
It connects submission to everything James has just exposed.
This is not merely a verse about confronting the devil.
It is a call to abandon proud, divided allegiance and return to God.
And perhaps that is why this passage can be so painful.
Because it forces us to ask a question we would rather avoid.
What if some of the things I keep calling spiritual attacks are also situations in which I need to repent, obey, seek help, or take responsibility?
Not every hardship is caused by personal sin.
Not every intrusive thought is a demonic attack.
Not every season of depression, anxiety, grief, or exhaustion means someone has failed to submit to God.
Scripture itself shows faithful people suffering deeply.
Job suffered without his suffering being explained as punishment for a hidden personal sin.
Paul endured affliction while remaining devoted to Christ.
Even Jesus, who was perfectly obedient, faced temptation and suffering.
So we must never turn James 4:7 into a weapon against hurting people.
But neither should we use the reality of spiritual warfare to avoid confronting our own choices.
Sometimes the issue is not that you need to shout louder.
Sometimes you need to tell the truth.
Sometimes you need to apologize.
Sometimes you need to delete the conversation.
Sometimes you need to stop entertaining the fantasy.
Sometimes you need to confess what you have hidden.
Sometimes you need to forgive, even while maintaining necessary boundaries.
Sometimes you need to seek pastoral counsel, professional support, or accountability instead of continuing to fight alone.
And sometimes the prayer that changes everything begins with five painfully honest words.
“Lord, I have been wrong.”
There is a kind of Christianity that wants the authority of Christ without the surrender of self.
We want Jesus to silence the storm, but we resist Him when He confronts the sin.
We want Him to protect our future, but we refuse to release our past.
We want Him to bless our relationships, but we do not want Him examining how we treat people.
We want Him to heal our hearts, but we keep returning to the very patterns that deepen our wounds.
We want victory.
But we struggle with surrender.
And perhaps the hardest thing about surrender is that it often feels like losing.
Losing control.
Losing the right to retaliate.
Losing the relationship we know is destroying us.
Losing the identity we built around our wounds.
Losing the secret pleasure we have defended for years.
Losing the illusion that we can follow Jesus while keeping certain rooms of our lives permanently locked.
Yet Jesus said:
“For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.” — Luke 9:24, KJV
The world tells you to protect yourself at all costs.
Jesus calls you to trust Him with your entire life.
And that is where the battle becomes deeply personal.
Imagine a man sitting alone in his car after another argument with his wife.
His hands are gripping the steering wheel.
His jaw is tight.
He is convinced that she is the problem.
He has already rehearsed every insult, every accusation, every painful thing he plans to say when he walks back through the door.
Then a familiar Scripture comes to mind.
“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
So he begins praying against the enemy.
But as he prays, another Scripture comes to mind.
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.” — James 1:19, KJV
Suddenly the question is no longer merely whether the devil is attacking his marriage.
The question is whether he is willing to obey God in the middle of his anger.
Will he listen?
Will he repent of cruel words?
Will he take responsibility without demanding that his wife confess first?
Will he choose humility when pride feels so much easier?
That is what surrender can look like.
Not dramatic.
Not impressive.
Not something that necessarily receives applause.
Just a man standing outside his own front door, realizing that following Jesus may require him to say something his pride has resisted for years.
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
And maybe, for that man, the battle begins to change when he stops trying to win the argument and starts obeying Christ.
Now imagine a woman lying awake at 2:17 in the morning.
The room is dark.
Her phone is glowing.
She has promised God so many times that she would stop returning to the same destructive relationship.
But tonight, loneliness feels unbearable.
The message is already typed.
All she has to do is press send.
She knows what will happen.
The brief comfort.
The emotional attachment.
The familiar compromise.
The shame afterward.
And once again, she whispers, “God, please help me.”
That prayer matters.
But perhaps the next act of faith is also painfully practical.
Putting the phone down.
Blocking the contact if necessary.
Calling a trustworthy friend tomorrow.
Choosing not to confuse loneliness with permission to return to harm.
Believing that obedience to Christ is worth more than a few moments of counterfeit comfort.
This is not salvation by human willpower.
This is what grace begins to produce in a life learning to walk with God.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God not only brings salvation but also trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not simply comfort us while leaving us unchanged.
Grace teaches us to live differently.
And here is where we must be especially careful.
Submission to God does not purchase His love. It is a response to the love He has already revealed in Jesus Christ.
You do not become worthy of Jesus by achieving perfect obedience.
You do not earn forgiveness by defeating every temptation.
You do not save yourself by becoming spiritually strong enough.
The Gospel is not the story of humanity climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the story of the Son of God coming down to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
That means the person who has fallen repeatedly is not beyond the reach of Christ.
The person ashamed of secret sin is not too filthy to approach Him.
The believer who is exhausted from fighting temptation does not have to pretend to be stronger than they are.
Jesus did not come to save people who could prove they had no need of a Savior.
He came for sinners.
And that changes the way we understand spiritual warfare.
Because before we look at how believers resist the devil, we need to look at the One who faced temptation without surrendering to sin.
Jesus Christ.
In Matthew 4:1–11, Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, where He was tempted by the devil.
He had fasted forty days and forty nights.
He was hungry.
Physically weakened.
Alone in the wilderness.
And the tempter approached Him.
“If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread.” — Matthew 4:3, KJV
Jesus answered with Scripture.
“Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.” — Matthew 4:4, KJV
The devil then tempted Him to put God to the test.
Again, Jesus answered from Scripture.
Then came the offer of the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship.
A crown without the cross.
Glory without obedience to the Father's will.
And Jesus answered:
“Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve.” — Matthew 4:10, KJV
Then Matthew records:
“Then the devil leaveth him, and, behold, angels came and ministered unto him.” — Matthew 4:11, KJV
Do you see the beauty of this?
Jesus did not negotiate with temptation.
He did not reshape God's Word to accommodate the enemy's offer.
He remained faithful to His Father.
But we must not reduce this encounter to a simple technique, as though quoting the right verses automatically ends every spiritual struggle.
Jesus was not merely demonstrating a method.
He was revealing Himself as the obedient Son.
Where Adam fell into disobedience, Christ remained faithful.
Where Israel repeatedly failed in the wilderness, Jesus obeyed.
And He continued that obedience all the way to the cross.
Philippians 2:8 tells us that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
That is the heart of our hope.
Our ultimate victory does not rest on the perfection of our resistance, but on the finished work of the Savior to whom we belong.
Colossians 2:13–15 describes God's forgiveness through Christ and Christ's triumph over hostile spiritual powers through the cross.
Hebrews 2:14–15 teaches that through His death, Jesus broke the devil's power over death and delivered those enslaved by the fear of death.
And 1 John 3:8 declares that the Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
The cross was not a tragic interruption of God's plan.
It was central to God's saving purpose.
The enemy tempted.
Humanity sinned.
Christ obeyed.
Christ suffered.
Christ died.
And Christ rose again.
That is why a Christian does not resist the devil in order to become their own savior.
A Christian resists by faith in the Savior who has already conquered sin and death.
But what does that resistance look like on an ordinary Tuesday?
When nobody is watching?
When temptation is quiet?
When the struggle is not dramatic enough for a testimony video?
It looks like trusting what God has said even when your feelings are screaming something different.
It looks like refusing a lie because you know the truth.
It looks like praying when you feel spiritually dry.
It looks like turning away from temptation rather than testing how close you can get.
It looks like refusing bitterness even when you have been genuinely wronged.
It looks like speaking truth instead of manipulating someone.
It looks like bringing hidden sin into the light with wise, trustworthy accountability.
It looks like putting on the whole armor of God described in Ephesians 6:10–18.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness given by the Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
Notice how much of biblical spiritual resistance involves a life anchored in God rather than a fascination with the devil.
The believer is not called to become obsessed with darkness.
The believer is called to stand firm in the Lord.
And when James says the devil will flee, we can trust God's Word without turning that promise into a guarantee that every temptation will disappear immediately or permanently.
The same Scriptures tell believers to remain watchful.
First Peter 5:8–9 says to be sober and vigilant, resisting the devil steadfast in the faith.
The Christian life includes ongoing vigilance.
Temptation may return.
Battles may continue.
A difficult season does not automatically mean your resistance has failed.
But through Christ, the devil does not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to God.
And you do not have to surrender to every temptation that knocks on the door of your mind.
There is another detail in James 4 that deserves our attention.
After saying, “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you,” James immediately writes:
There it is.
The heart of the passage.
Not simply getting away from the devil.
Drawing near to God.
James continues by calling sinners to cleanse their hands and the double-minded to purify their hearts.
He calls for genuine sorrow over sin and humility before the Lord.
And then comes another promise:
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” — James 4:10, KJV
What a beautiful contrast.
The proud heart wants to lift itself up.
The humble heart bows before God.
And God promises to lift up the humble.
The Greek word translated “double minded” in James 4:8 is δίψυχοι (dipsychoi), describing those divided in loyalty or purpose.
That word reaches into places we do not like discussing.
Because it is possible to sing about surrender on Sunday while carefully protecting disobedience throughout the week.
It is possible to say Jesus is Lord while treating His commands as optional whenever they become inconvenient.
It is possible to want God's blessings without wanting God's authority.
But Jesus does not call us into a half-hearted arrangement.
He calls us to Himself.
And perhaps someone reading this is beginning to feel exposed.
Not because a stranger on the internet knows your secrets.
But because Scripture has reached a place in your heart that you have kept hidden.
Maybe it is the addiction.
Maybe it is the affair nobody knows about.
Maybe it is the unforgiveness that has become part of your personality.
Maybe it is the constant need to be admired.
Maybe it is the dishonest business practice you have learned to justify.
Maybe it is the pornography you keep promising to abandon.
Maybe it is the spiritual pride that makes you quick to correct others but slow to confess your own sins.
Maybe it is the bitterness toward God because life did not unfold the way you prayed it would.
Or maybe you are simply tired.
Tired of falling.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of smiling in church while secretly wondering whether God could still want someone like you.
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
Conviction is not an invitation to run away from Jesus. It is a reason to run toward Him.
The enemy would have you believe that your sin is too ugly to confess and your history too damaged to redeem.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Remember Peter.
He was confident.
Bold.
Certain of his loyalty.
He insisted that even if others abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing his Lord.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And Luke records one of the most heartbreaking moments in the Gospels.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that look.
Peter had just denied the One he loved.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter remembered.
Luke 22:62 says he went out and wept bitterly.
Have you ever had a moment like that?
A moment when your own actions suddenly became impossible to excuse?
When the excuses collapsed?
When you realized that you had betrayed the very values you claimed to believe?
When you wished you could rewind time and choose differently?
Peter knew that pain.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus met His disciples by the Sea of Tiberias.
And in John 21, Jesus addressed Peter personally.
Three times He asked Peter about his love.
Three times Peter responded.
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had publicly denied Christ was not discarded as useless.
He was restored and commissioned by the risen Savior.
That is grace.
Not pretending the denial never happened.
Not calling betrayal acceptable.
Not erasing the seriousness of sin.
But restoring a repentant disciple through the mercy and authority of Jesus Christ.
Peter's failure was real. But Jesus had not finished writing Peter's story.
And maybe He has not finished writing yours.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because brokenness should be celebrated.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem what sin has devastated.
He can forgive the guilty.
Restore the repentant.
Transform the proud.
Strengthen the weary.
And give new life to those who come to Him in faith.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That does not mean every consequence disappears overnight.
It does not mean damaged trust is instantly repaired.
It does not mean healing always follows our preferred timetable.
But it does mean that your past does not have the authority to define your identity forever when you belong to Jesus Christ.
And this is why the call to submit to God is not bad news.
It is the doorway into a life of trusting the One who loves us enough to confront what is destroying us.
Consider the father who finally admits he needs help with his anger.
The mother who stops measuring her worth by whether everyone approves of her.
The young man who confesses his secret struggle and begins seeking godly accountability.
The young woman who realizes she does not need to compromise her convictions to be loved.
The pastor who humbles himself enough to acknowledge that he too needs correction, prayer, and grace.
The person who has spent years blaming everyone else and finally asks, “Lord, what must change in me?”
These moments may never go viral.
They may never be seen by thousands.
But heaven does not measure spiritual significance by social media attention.
And obedience performed quietly before God is not wasted.
Maybe your next breakthrough will not begin with a spectacular experience.
Maybe it will begin with a surrendered heart.
A truthful confession.
An overdue apology.
A difficult boundary.
A decision to seek help.
A Bible opened after months of neglect.
A whispered prayer from someone who has run out of excuses.
“Jesus, I cannot keep living this way. Have mercy on me. Teach me to follow You.”
And if you are wondering whether Jesus will receive a sinner who comes to Him, listen to His own words:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
What an extraordinary promise.
Not “I will receive you once you have fixed yourself.”
Not “I will welcome you after you prove that you will never fail again.”
But a gracious assurance from the Savior Himself.
Come to Me.
That is where transformation begins.
Not with self-righteous confidence.
Not with spiritual performance.
But with repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
And repentance is more than feeling terrible about what you have done.
It involves turning from sin toward God.
The New Testament often uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, referring to a change of mind and heart that is expressed in a changed direction of life.
True repentance is not merely saying, “I am sorry I got caught.”
It is recognizing sin for what it is and turning toward the God whose mercy we desperately need.
And when we fall, we do not have to hide.
First John 1:9 tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Christian life is not a life of pretending to be sinless.
It is a life of walking in the light, trusting Christ, confessing sin, and growing in obedience by God's grace.
Perhaps you have been resisting the devil in your prayers while resisting God in your decisions.
If so, do not use this realization as another reason to hate yourself.
Let it become a reason to humble yourself before the Lord.
Because the same passage that commands submission also declares that God gives more grace.
More grace.
For the proud person willing to humble themselves.
For the wandering believer willing to return.
For the exhausted disciple who needs strength.
For the sinner who has finally stopped defending the sin.
Not permission to continue in darkness.
Grace to come into the light.
And if you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ, this invitation is for you too.
You do not need a religious performance.
You need the Savior.
Jesus died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures, as Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him as Lord.
And if you have belonged to Christ for years but have been living with a divided heart, today is a good day to return to honest obedience.
You do not need to impress God with elaborate words.
You can pray sincerely, right where you are.
“Father, I have spent so much time asking You to change what is happening around me while resisting what You want to change within me.
Forgive me for the sins I have defended, the pride I have protected, and the compromises I have excused.
Lord Jesus, thank You for dying for sinners and rising again.
I believe that Your mercy is greater than my ability to repair my own life.
Teach me to submit to You.
Give me strength to resist temptation.
Help me love what is good and turn away from what is evil.
Show me where I need to repent, whom I need to forgive, and where I need to make things right.
When I am weak, remind me that Your grace is sufficient.
When I stumble, lead me back into the light.
When the enemy accuses me, anchor my hope in Your finished work, not in my own perfection.
And when I am tempted to take control again, teach me to trust You.
I surrender myself to You, Jesus.
Not because I am strong.
But because You are faithful.
Amen.”
If that prayer reflects the battle in your heart, I want to ask you something.
Not for appearances.
Not to prove your spirituality to strangers.
But because there is something powerful about refusing to pretend anymore.
Would you be willing to be honest about where you are in your walk with Christ?
You do not need to expose private details or share anything that could put you at risk.
A simple, honest comment is enough.
Someone reading may be convinced that their story is beyond redemption, and your testimony could remind them of the mercy of Christ.
Think about the people in your life.
The brother who seems fine but is quietly losing his battle with temptation.
The sister who smiles through worship but cries herself to sleep.
The friend who has stopped attending church because shame convinced them they no longer belong.
The father whose anger is destroying his family.
The young person who believes they have already gone too far for God to forgive.
The believer who keeps quoting the promise but has never seriously considered the command that comes first.
Maybe this article is not only for you.
Maybe someone else needs to hear it too.
A believer who needs strengthening.
A seeker with honest questions.
A person who has grown distant from church.
Even someone who does not yet believe in Jesus.
Let them encounter a message that does not hide the seriousness of sin or the extraordinary mercy of Christ.
And if this ministry has been feeding your faith, I want to share something close to our heart.
Gospel Warrior is not simply about publishing words that stir emotions for a few minutes.

Our desire is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, confront sin honestly, experience the comfort of God's promises, and become more faithful disciples of Jesus Christ.
That takes ongoing work.
Writing.
Research.
Biblical study.
Resource development.
And the effort to keep reaching people who may be one message away from opening Scripture again.
We want those resources to remain accessible to people who cannot afford expensive books or study materials.
It is a voluntary way to give in support of Gospel-centered work.
But we also want to be clear about something important.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It can help us continue producing Scripture-centered articles like this one, expanding free Christian resources, and reaching people who need to hear the Gospel.
These products can also serve as reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to start meaningful conversations about Jesus.
You are welcome here.
Read the free resources.
Study the Scriptures.
Pray for the ministry.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Your worth in Christ is not measured by what you can afford.
Because one day, the posts will stop appearing on our screens.
The likes will be forgotten.
The numbers will no longer matter.
But the Word of God will endure.
And what matters most is not whether we built an impressive platform.
It is whether we were faithful to the truth of Jesus Christ.
Whether we pointed people toward repentance and grace.
Whether we cared for the wounded without excusing sin.
Whether we proclaimed Christ rather than ourselves.
Whether those who encountered our work were encouraged to know and follow the Savior.
That is the kind of mission worth supporting.
And now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to where we started.
James 4:7.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Maybe you came into this article expecting another message about how to make the devil run.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit has used Scripture to show you something more personal.
A habit that needs to end.
A confession that needs to be made.
A relationship that needs wise boundaries.
A wound that needs healing.
A proud attitude that needs to bow.
A secret that needs to come into the light.
A Savior you need to trust more deeply.
Do not ignore what God's Word has brought to your attention.
Do not settle for feeling convicted today and remaining unchanged tomorrow.
Take one faithful step.
Not to earn the love of Jesus.
But because Jesus is worthy of your whole life.
And remember, the command to resist the devil was never meant to distract you from the greater invitation.
Draw near to God.
He is not asking you to defeat darkness by your own strength.
He is calling you to stand firm in the grace and truth of the One who has already overcome.
The devil is not your savior.
Your willpower is not your savior.
Your religious reputation is not your savior.
Jesus Christ is your Savior.
So when temptation comes again, remember whose you are.
When shame whispers that you are beyond forgiveness, remember the cross.
When pride tells you that surrender is weakness, remember the humility of Christ.
When you stumble, repent and return to Him.
When you are exhausted, draw near to Him.
And when the enemy tries to convince you that your past is the end of your story, remember Peter standing before the risen Jesus.
The denial was not erased from history.
But it did not have the final word.
Jesus did.
And if you remember only one thing from everything you have read today, let it be this:
You have spent so long asking the devil to leave that you may have forgotten Jesus is calling you to come closer.
